previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old woman was admitted with coffee ground emesis and abdominal pain, two days after discharge from rehab for a gout flare. Evaluation revealed stable hemoglobin with a brief drop, leading to concern for a mild upper GI bleed. Imaging showed a large hiatal hernia with intrathoracic stomach and delayed gastric emptying, but no obstruction or diverticulitis. Endoscopy confirmed esophagitis as a likely source of bleeding. She was treated with IV pantoprazole, advanced to oral intake, and her symptoms improved. Acute kidney injury, likely pre-renal from reduced intake and contrast, resolved with hydration. Hypokalemia was corrected with supplementation. Her chronic thrombocytopenia remained stable. She was discharged home with plans for outpatient cardiac stress testing, surgical evaluation for hiatal hernia repair, and follow-up for kidney lesions and esophagitis.
problems: Diaphragmatic hernia without mention of obstruction or gangrene

Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted for evaluation of left axillary pain. EKG and 
lab tests showed that you did not have a heart attack. You also 
underwent a stress test which was normal. The pain you 
experienced is likely musculoskeletal in nature, since it hurts 
more when pressed in the area and when you move. It should 
improve with time. Since you have a history of bleeding in the 
gut, do not take any NSAIDs such as Advil and Motrin. We are 
giving you some pain medication to help with the pain along with 
Tylenol.

Please call your doctor or return to the emergency room if you 
experience chest pain/pressure, pain radiating to the jaw or 
left shoulder, shortness of breath, nausea/vomiting, 
lightheadedness, or any other symptoms that concern you.
